Re: referencing nodes by id, how to set global vars?
I think that you should be able to make it a static class, since `id`
is defined as being "tag only, and final" which means that it cannot
be set at run time (even though that is how it is presently
implemented). I would hope that by making it a static class, the JS2
compiler can completely optimize away the dynamic lookup that the
`with` would otherwise imply.

BUT: there is one other "gotcha" I forgot to mention as to why you
can't "wrap every function's contents with 'with (global)'". Consider
the following:

code
code
code
Should yield `-3`, but if you take the simple approach of wrapping
`with (global)`, will yield `42`. (And similarly for the instance and
class `foo` if the closer binding were not present.)

The compiler already also can tell you about closed-over variables,
so, I think the best solution is to simply rewrite free references (to
global.foo) when they match declared id's (which the tag compiler can
tell the script compiler in advance, because it is going to put them
in a static class with a singleton instance). The one additional
piece of analysis that is needed is to find the instance (including
inherited) and class variables that could match the free reference --
those should not be rewritten, but I'm not sure the compiler takes
those into account when doing its analysis.

Re: For Review: Change 41085 Summary:Remove string-parametric property access from width/height dependent
I sent some code to this list last week that might be useful for
this. It contained a version of _lookups with all the properties
referenced in these functions, and some of the changes necessary to
use this lookup table.

Jim measured this and, to my surprise, it wasn't faster on Flash. I
guess the moral of this is that it's worth measuring whether the
change actually improves performance on some specific runtime, rather
than assuming that it might.

However, there's an additional complexity that I just thought of.
The full cost of string construction might not show up in a profiler
because part of the cost is the increased object churn, which dials
up the gc frequency, and a profiling run wouldn't show this unless it
was long enough to trigger a statistically accurate number gcs. So a
table-driven approach, which substitutes the cost of hashing for the
cost of string construction, might still be faster over the long term
even if it measures out the same in a short run, by replacing string
allocation (pay not AND pay later) with hash lookup (pay only now).

By using a plain signature, yes, you are saying that you are willing to
- - shall we say - publically say this key is valid. As in, the rest of
the Internet should trust that you say this key is valid.

quotation
Not sure what this is... However, the reason you'd remove a sig from
your key is if a particular person proves somehow to be unreliable to
such an extent that keys signed by this persons key are viewed with
increased distrust...

Example 1, say person A has a key and his friend person B knows for a
fact that person A owns key A and keeps it secure. Person B does some
kind of man in the middle attack on someone using a false key that they
have signed by their key, Key B. Person A may not want their key
associated with person B anymore.

Example 2, same two people, but person B's key is stolen and used to
sign a lot of keys that are used for less than honest purposes (man in
the middle attack stuff) and person A, once more, doesn't want their key
associated at all with person B's key (while not specifically person B).

In addition, why you'd want to restrict that is if you are in a company
and you want to make sure that employee's use their business key for
business purposes you may force your corperate sig to stay on their key
so that they can't use it for nonbusiness purposes without immediately
associating it with the business.

quotation
Exactly, you are saying by doing a local sig that you believe this
person is who they say they are, but you aren't positive enough to say
that the rest of the Internet should trust it because you do.

Re: Problems starting wmii
quotation
I just did an update and ran into the same problem as Frank.

After doing a little bit of research, I found that rci doesn't handle
commands of the form in the same way as bash does.

For example, when bash sees a " -r ~/.wmii/rc ", it executes "[ -r
~/.wmii/rc". When rci sees " -r ~/.wmii/rc ", it executes " -r
~/.wmii/rc ". The command (which is a symlink to the test command)
doesn't like being passed those extra 's.

The easiet way to "fix" it is to remove the ]'s from any [ evaluations.
That, of course, makes all the if statements look lopsided.

I don't know if it's Frank and my's version of test that's bringing this
issue to light or what. I just know what caused it ;)
